lines.title: Intro
lines.text: Hey, I'm Taylor, and I'm a real person.

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: I'm also a user experience and product designer,

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: and I'd like to show you something I've been working on.

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: It's called Color Taylor.

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: I'll just move myself out of the way, for now.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I used to struggle with picking colors using RGB.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: In time, I found hue and saturation models were helpful for dialing in the colors I want.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Let's say I have this turquoise,

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: but I want to get it to teal,

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: which is a harmonious, but darker color.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: How do I dial that into RGB?

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I think I need to lower the red

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: and the blue,

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: but how much do I change the RGB before I stray too far from my source?

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Once I understood how hue models and RGB work together,

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I could more confidently understand how colors were constructed.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: There, that's teal.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Our focus for this presentation will be on hue, saturation, and brightness.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: This app supports HSL as well, so you can use what's familiar to you.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Color Taylor is meant to be a playground and educational tool for how RGB and HSB work together.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: You see the relationships in real time,

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: which can strengthen your understanding of how colors work on displays.

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: The color editor on the right should be familiar to most people who have worked with creative tools.

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: The hexagon on the left is a different way of displaying the same information.

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: Around the hexagon we have the Hue,

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: which is an angle that ranges from 0

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: to 360 degrees.

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: Red is 0...

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: green is 120...

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: and blue is 240.

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: By laying the primary colors out like this,

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: we can visualize how RGB values determine a color's hue.

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: Drag the handles around and you see how

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: red, green, and blue combine to make a color.

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: You'll notice on the hexagon between each of the primary colors, we see combinations:

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: yellow, which is red and green combined;

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: cyan, which is green and blue combined;

lines.title: The hexagon and hue
lines.text: and magenta, which is blue and red combined.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: Let's use an orangey color as a reference point,

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: Around 30 degrees we'll always have this warm tone between red and yellow.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: At the highest saturation and brightness the color will be a combination of

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: 2 parts red,

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: 1 part green,

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: 0 parts blue.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Saturation determines how colorful a color is.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: 100% saturation, like what we have here,

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: means the highest and lowest values are as far apart as they can be.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Desaturating reduces the range between red, green, and blue proportionally.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: When all three values are equal, there's no saturation, and you're left with gray.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Adding saturation increases the range between values.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Saturation scales off the highest value.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: For this orange, it's red, which holds still.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Green and blue move towards red or away from it

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: as we move the saturation slider.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Notice that the hue didn't change, only the range between RGB values changed.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: We're still at hue 30, which is the same orangey source color we started with.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Brightness determines how light or dark a color is.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: The highest RGB value sets the brightness.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: As we adjust the brightness,

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: the hue and saturation are maintained.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: This is done by scaling the RGB values proportionally off of zero.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: At 100% brightness the hexagon is at its largest.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: As we lower the brightness, the hexagon contracts,

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: and red, green, and blue stems shorten with it,

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: keeping the same angles and proportions.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Notice we stay at the same 30 degree orangey color while moving the brightness.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: We'll use the swatches section to show how we can use HSB to set six different variations of the same hue.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: We can use HSB to come up with a bright desaturated orange,

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: then go down the scale until we have a dark vibrant variant.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: This is hinting at what a design system might do.

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: We've been exploring the playground,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: but if you want the classroom perspective,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: check out the equations section.

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: It shows the math behind

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: hue,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: saturation,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: brightness,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: as well as how Hex and normalized colors are calculated.

lines.title: Handoff to the demo
lines.text: Now we can move on to the demo.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Start with the sliders and controls you already know.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Moving one slider will highlight every other slider it affects.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Click the droplet button to switch between source or mixed color sliders.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Click the tags button to show HTML colors on the hexagon.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Drag a handle on the hexagon and watch the RGB and HSB sliders follow.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Have fun exploring and learning about different color models.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: If you use Figma, I've also made a Color Taylor plugin that you might like to check out.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: That's Color Taylor!

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: Go play with it, and I hope it helps you see the relationship between RGB and HSB in a different light.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: If it's useful, I'd like to hear from you. Questions and feedback are welcome.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: Thanks for watching. See ya.
